title: Crypto History & Legendary Token Stories
subtitle: Learn from the Most Iconic Projects in Cryptocurrency

intro.title: Introduction: Learning from Crypto History
intro.content:
Every legendary token has a story—of innovation, triumph, failure, and lessons learned. This guide explores the most iconic projects in cryptocurrency history, from Bitcoin's revolutionary whitepaper to the rise and fall of algorithmic stablecoins.

Understanding crypto history isn't just about nostalgia. These stories reveal timeless patterns: what makes a project successful, what causes spectacular failures, and how the industry evolves. Whether you're investing, building, or simply curious, these lessons are invaluable.

We'll explore both the legendary successes that changed the industry and the infamous failures that taught us hard lessons. Each story offers insights that remain relevant today.

bitcoin.title: Bitcoin: The Origin Story
bitcoin.content: Bitcoin didn't just create a new currency—it sparked a revolution in money, technology, and trust. Understanding Bitcoin's journey from a cryptography mailing list post to a trillion-dollar asset class is essential for understanding all of crypto.

satoshi.title: Satoshi Nakamoto and the Whitepaper
satoshi.content:
On October 31, 2008, someone using the pseudonym Satoshi Nakamoto published a whitepaper titled "Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System" on a cryptography mailing list. The timing was perfect—just weeks after the 2008 financial crisis began.

The whitepaper proposed a radical solution to a long-standing problem in computer science: how to create digital money without a central authority. Previous attempts at digital currencies had failed because they required someone to prevent double-spending (using the same money twice).

Satoshi's innovation was proof-of-work combined with a distributed ledger. Instead of trusting a bank, you trust mathematics and a network of computers that verify transactions. The network reaches consensus on the order of transactions, making double-spending impossible without controlling 51% of the network's computing power.

On January 3, 2009, Satoshi mined the genesis block—Bitcoin's first block. The coinbase parameter contained the message: "The Times 03/Jan/2009 Chancellor on brink of second bailout for banks." This wasn't just a timestamp—it was a statement of purpose.

milestones.title: Key Bitcoin Milestones
milestones.content:
First Transaction (January 12, 2009): Satoshi sent 10 BTC to Hal Finney, a cryptographer and early Bitcoin contributor. This was the first person-to-person Bitcoin transaction.

First Real-World Purchase (May 22, 2010): Laszlo Hanyecz paid 10,000 BTC for two pizzas—now celebrated as "Bitcoin Pizza Day." At today's prices, those pizzas would be worth hundreds of millions of dollars.

Mt. Gox Era (2010-2014): Mt. Gox became the dominant Bitcoin exchange, handling 70% of all Bitcoin transactions at its peak. Its catastrophic collapse in 2014 (850,000 BTC stolen) was Bitcoin's first major crisis, teaching the industry hard lessons about custody and security.

First Halving (November 28, 2012): Bitcoin's mining reward dropped from 50 BTC to 25 BTC per block. This event, programmed into Bitcoin's code, occurs every 210,000 blocks (roughly four years). Halvings create Bitcoin's deflationary monetary policy—only 21 million BTC will ever exist.

Reaching $1,000 (November 2013): Bitcoin's price crossed $1,000 for the first time, attracting mainstream media attention and legitimacy.

$10,000 and Beyond (2017-2021): Bitcoin reached $10,000 in 2017, $20,000 in late 2017, crashed to $3,000 in 2018, then surged to $69,000 in November 2021. Each cycle brought new investors, infrastructure, and understanding.

impact.title: Bitcoin's Impact on Finance
impact.content:
Bitcoin proved that decentralized digital money was possible. But its impact goes far beyond payments:

Store of Value: Bitcoin evolved from "peer-to-peer cash" to "digital gold." Its fixed supply makes it attractive as a hedge against inflation. Institutional investors now hold Bitcoin on their balance sheets.

Financial Sovereignty: Bitcoin enables anyone to be their own bank. In countries with unstable currencies or authoritarian regimes, Bitcoin provides financial freedom. No government can freeze a self-custody Bitcoin wallet.

Blockchain Technology: Bitcoin introduced the blockchain—a distributed, immutable ledger. This technology inspired thousands of projects, from Ethereum's smart contracts to enterprise blockchain solutions.

Proof of Concept: Bitcoin proved that a global, decentralized currency could work without a central authority. Every cryptocurrency that followed builds on this foundation.

By 2024, Bitcoin has achieved what seemed impossible in 2009: recognition as a legitimate asset class. Governments regulate it, institutions invest in it, and millions of people hold it. Satoshi Nakamoto remains anonymous, but their creation changed the world.

ethereum.title: Ethereum: The World Computer
ethereum.content: If Bitcoin is digital gold, Ethereum is digital infrastructure. Vitalik Buterin's vision of programmable blockchain created an entire ecosystem of decentralized applications, from DeFi to NFTs to DAOs.

vitalik_vision.title: Vitalik Buterin and the Smart Contract Vision
vitalik_vision.content:
In late 2013, 19-year-old Vitalik Buterin published the Ethereum whitepaper, proposing a blockchain with a built-in Turing-complete programming language. Bitcoin's scripting was intentionally limited; Ethereum would be unlimited.

The vision was ambitious: a "world computer" where anyone could deploy unstoppable applications. Smart contracts—programs that execute automatically when conditions are met—would replace intermediaries in finance, governance, and beyond.

Ethereum's ICO (Initial Coin Offering) in July-August 2014 raised 31,529 BTC (~$18 million), selling ETH at about $0.30. The network launched on July 30, 2015, with 72 million ETH in the genesis block.

Early adoption was slow. Ethereum needed killer apps to demonstrate its potential. Those apps would emerge in 2017 with ICOs and in 2020 with DeFi.

dao_hack.title: The DAO Hack and Hard Fork
dao_hack.content:
In April 2016, a group launched The DAO—a decentralized autonomous organization for venture capital. It was ambitious: a organization governed entirely by code, where token holders voted on investments.

The DAO's crowdfunding broke records, raising 12.7 million ETH (about $150 million at the time)—14% of all ETH in existence. But the code had a critical vulnerability.

June 17, 2016: An attacker exploited a reentrancy bug, draining 3.6 million ETH (~$50 million) into a child DAO. The Ethereum community faced an impossible choice: uphold "code is law" and let the hacker keep the funds, or intervene and reverse the theft.

After intense debate, the community voted for a hard fork—essentially rewinding the blockchain to before the hack. On July 20, 2016, Ethereum split into two chains:

  • Ethereum (ETH): The majority chain that reversed the hack
  • Ethereum Classic (ETC): The minority chain that kept the original history

The DAO hack taught crucial lessons about smart contract security. It also raised philosophical questions about immutability and governance that the industry still grapples with today.

pos_transition.title: The Merge: Transitioning to Proof of Stake
pos_transition.content:
For years, Ethereum ran on Proof of Work (PoW)—the same consensus mechanism as Bitcoin. Miners competed to solve cryptographic puzzles, consuming enormous amounts of electricity. This was always meant to be temporary.

The plan was to transition to Proof of Stake (PoS), where validators "stake" ETH instead of burning electricity. PoS would be more energy-efficient, more scalable, and more secure.

The transition took far longer than expected. Originally planned for 2017, delays and technical challenges pushed it back repeatedly. The Ethereum community joked about it being "18 months away" for years.

September 15, 2022—The Merge: After years of development and testing, Ethereum successfully transitioned to PoS. The network's energy consumption dropped by 99.95% overnight. It was one of the most technically ambitious upgrades in crypto history—like changing a plane's engines mid-flight.

The Merge proved that even the second-largest blockchain could make radical changes through community consensus. It set the stage for future upgrades focused on scalability and user experience.

defi_summer.title: DeFi Summer: The 2020 Revolution
defi_summer.content: Summer 2020 saw an explosion of innovation in Decentralized Finance (DeFi). Suddenly, anyone could earn yield, provide liquidity, and access financial services without banks or brokers. DeFi Summer created legendary protocols that still dominate today.

compound.title: Compound: The Spark That Lit DeFi Summer
compound.content:
Compound wasn't the first DeFi lending protocol, but its June 2020 decision to distribute COMP governance tokens to users sparked a phenomenon: yield farming.

The mechanism was simple: deposit assets into Compound, earn interest, plus receive COMP tokens worth potentially more than the interest. COMP launched at ~$60 and quickly shot to $372 within days.

This created a feedback loop: COMP tokens had value because people deposited into Compound, and people deposited into Compound to earn COMP. The protocol's TVL (Total Value Locked) exploded from $100 million to over $1 billion in weeks.

More importantly, Compound proved a model: liquidity mining. Protocols could attract users and liquidity by distributing governance tokens. This model spread across DeFi, defining the summer of 2020.

Lessons learned: Token incentives can bootstrap network effects rapidly, but they must be sustainable. Many protocols that copied Compound's model without substance collapsed when rewards dried up.

uniswap.title: Uniswap: AMM Innovation
uniswap.content:
Uniswap, launched in November 2018 by Hayden Adams, introduced the Automated Market Maker (AMM) model to Ethereum. Instead of order books, Uniswap used liquidity pools and a simple constant-product formula: x × y = k.

Early adoption was slow. Why use Uniswap when centralized exchanges were faster and had better prices? But Uniswap offered something unique: anyone could list any token instantly, without permission.

During DeFi Summer, Uniswap became essential infrastructure. New tokens launched on Uniswap. Yield farmers swapped between protocols on Uniswap. Volume exploded.

September 2020: Uniswap surprised everyone with a retroactive airdrop—400 UNI tokens (~$1,200 at the time) to anyone who had ever used the protocol. This was one of crypto's most generous airdrops, rewarding early users and creating intense loyalty.

Uniswap proved that DeFi could compete with centralized exchanges. By 2021, Uniswap V3 handled more volume than most centralized exchanges, with zero downtime and no KYC.

aave.title: Aave: Flash Loans and Innovation
aave.content:
Aave (originally ETHLend) evolved from a struggling ICO project into one of DeFi's most innovative lending protocols. Its key innovation? Flash loans.

Flash loans let anyone borrow millions of dollars with zero collateral—as long as they repay within the same transaction. If they can't repay, the entire transaction reverts, as if the loan never happened.

This sounds absurd, but it unlocked powerful use cases: instant arbitrage, collateral swaps, and self-liquidations. Flash loans democratized strategies that previously required massive capital.

Aave also innovated in other ways: rate switching (swap between fixed and variable rates), credit delegation (uncollateralized loans based on trust), and multi-collateral support.

By listening to users and iterating rapidly, Aave grew from a struggling project to one of DeFi's blue chips. Its TVL reached over $20 billion at its peak, making it one of the largest lending protocols.

nft_revolution.title: The NFT Revolution
nft_revolution.content: Non-Fungible Tokens (NFTs) existed for years before exploding into mainstream consciousness in 2021. These digital collectibles created new economies for artists, communities, and speculators.

cryptopunks.title: CryptoPunks: The OGs
cryptopunks.content:
In June 2017, Larva Labs released CryptoPunks—10,000 unique 24×24 pixel characters as an experiment in digital scarcity on Ethereum. They were free to claim (just pay gas), and most people ignored them.

CryptoPunks predated the ERC-721 NFT standard. They used their own contract, making them technically imperfect but historically significant. Early adopters claimed multiple Punks for pennies in gas fees.

Fast forward to 2021: NFTs exploded, and CryptoPunks became status symbols. Rare Punks (aliens, apes, zombies) sold for millions. Visa bought CryptoPunk #7610 for $150,000. Celebrities posted Punks as profile pictures.

By 2023, the cheapest Punk cost over $100,000. Total sales exceeded $2 billion. CryptoPunks proved that digital scarcity could create real value and that being first mattered enormously.

bayc.title: Bored Ape Yacht Club: Community and Utility
bayc.content:
In April 2021, Yuga Labs launched Bored Ape Yacht Club (BAYC)—10,000 unique ape NFTs at 0.08 ETH each (~$200 at launch). The pitch: owning an Ape granted membership to an exclusive club with events, merchandise, and future benefits.

BAYC didn't just sell JPEGs—they built a brand and community. Holders got commercial rights to their Apes, spawning businesses, merchandise, and derivative projects. The "Bored Ape" trademark became valuable in itself.

Celebrity adoption accelerated: Steph Curry, Eminem, Jimmy Fallon, and Paris Hilton bought Apes. Floor prices rocketed from 0.08 ETH to over 100 ETH (~$400,000) at the peak in April 2022.

Yuga Labs continued innovating: airdropping free Mutant Apes to holders, launching the Otherside metaverse, and acquiring CryptoPunks and Meebits. They raised $450 million at a $4 billion valuation.

BAYC proved that NFTs could be more than art—they could be memberships, brands, and communities. However, the bear market of 2022-2023 showed that hype alone isn't sustainable. Floor prices fell 90% from peaks, though BAYC remained a blue-chip collection.

opensea.title: OpenSea: The NFT Marketplace Wars
opensea.content:
OpenSea, founded in 2017, became the dominant NFT marketplace by 2021. During the NFT boom, OpenSea processed billions in monthly volume with minimal competition.

But dominance breeds complacency. OpenSea delayed launching a token while taking 2.5% fees. Competitors emerged: LooksRare launched with token rewards, Blur launched with trader incentives and zero fees for collections.

The Blur Challenge: In February 2023, Blur airdropped tokens to NFT traders, including OpenSea users. Blur's aggressive liquidity mining attracted professional traders, and its volume briefly exceeded OpenSea's.

OpenSea responded by reducing fees and improving features, but the damage was done. The NFT marketplace was no longer a monopoly—competition had arrived.

Lessons: Market leadership requires constant innovation. Failing to reward loyal users creates opportunities for competitors. In crypto, someone is always trying to disrupt you.

l2_altl1.title: Layer 2s and Alternative L1s
l2_altl1.content: As Ethereum fees soared in 2020-2021, alternatives emerged. Some built Layer 2 solutions on Ethereum; others created new Layer 1 blockchains. These stories showcase different approaches to blockchain scaling.

solana.title: Solana: Rise, Fall, and Resilience
solana.content:
Solana launched in March 2020 with an audacious vision: a blockchain that could handle thousands of transactions per second with sub-second finality, all while keeping fees under $0.01.

The technology was impressive: Proof of History (PoH) combined with Proof of Stake enabled unprecedented throughput. Solana called itself the "Ethereum killer," offering speed and low costs that Ethereum couldn't match.

The Rise (2021): Solana's ecosystem exploded. NFT projects like Degenerate Apes launched, DeFi protocols appeared, and SOL price rocketed from $1 to $260. FTX and Alameda Research heavily backed Solana, adding legitimacy and liquidity.

The Fall (2022): Network outages plagued Solana—the network halted multiple times, requiring validator coordination to restart. Then FTX collapsed in November 2022, and Solana's association with FTX became a liability. SOL crashed from $35 to $8.

The Resilience (2023-2024): Solana's community refused to give up. Despite outages and the FTX stigma, developers kept building. The memecoin boom on Solana in late 2023 brought activity back. By 2024, SOL recovered to $100+, and Solana proved it could survive crises.

Lessons: Technology alone isn't enough—reliability matters. Association risk is real (FTX nearly killed Solana). Strong communities can survive devastating setbacks.

arbitrum_optimism.title: Arbitrum and Optimism: The L2 Race
arbitrum_optimism.content:
Rather than competing with Ethereum, Arbitrum and Optimism chose to scale it. Both use optimistic rollups—executing transactions off-chain but inheriting Ethereum's security.

Optimism launched first (June 2021) with a cautious whitelist approach. It championed retroactive public goods funding, using protocol fees to fund Ethereum ecosystem projects. OP token launched in May 2022, distributed partially to users.

Arbitrum launched in August 2021 with a more aggressive approach: immediate public access, better EVM compatibility, and no token initially. Arbitrum's TVL quickly exceeded Optimism's as projects migrated.

The competition drove innovation: faster withdrawals, lower fees, better tooling. When Arbitrum finally launched ARB token in March 2023, it airdropped to users who'd bridged before a snapshot, rewarding early adopters.

By 2024, both protocols were thriving, but Arbitrum led in TVL and activity. The L2 wars proved that Ethereum's scaling strategy worked—L2s could offer low fees while maintaining security.

failures.title: Failures and Hard Lessons
failures.content: Crypto's failures are as important as its successes. These cautionary tales reveal what can go wrong and how to avoid similar mistakes.

luna_ust.title: Luna/UST: The Algorithmic Stablecoin Collapse
luna_ust.content:
Terra's algorithmic stablecoin UST and its sister token LUNA seemed like the future in early 2022. UST maintained its $1 peg through arbitrage with LUNA, without traditional collateral.

The mechanism: if UST fell below $1, users could burn 1 UST to mint $1 worth of LUNA (profit from arbitrage). If UST rose above $1, users could burn $1 of LUNA to mint 1 UST. This two-way burn-and-mint was supposed to keep UST stable.

Terra's ecosystem flourished: Anchor Protocol offered 20% APY on UST deposits, attracting billions. LUNA price soared from $5 to $119. Do Kwon, Terra's founder, became crypto's most confident (some said arrogant) personality.

May 7-12, 2022—The Death Spiral: A large UST holder began selling, causing UST to depeg slightly. Panic selling accelerated the depeg. As UST fell below $1, the arbitrage mechanism minted LUNA at an accelerating rate, hyperinflating LUNA's supply.

LUNA's price collapsed from $80 to $0.0001 in days. UST depegged entirely, falling to $0.10. Over $40 billion in market cap evaporated. Thousands lost their life savings.

Lessons:

  • Algorithmic stablecoins require perfect mechanism design and enormous liquidity
  • 20% sustainable yields don't exist—Anchor was subsidized and unsustainable
  • Confidence and arrogance are not substitutes for risk management
  • Death spirals can happen when systems rely on reflexive value

case_study.title: The Terra/Luna Collapse
case_study.description: In May 2022, Terra's algorithmic stablecoin UST depegged from $1, triggering a death spiral that destroyed $40 billion in value within days. The collapse exposed the fundamental fragility of algorithmic stablecoins backed only by market confidence rather than real collateral.

ftx.title: FTX: Centralization Risk
ftx.content:
FTX was crypto's golden child. Sam Bankman-Fried (SBF) built a leading exchange, secured celebrity endorsements (Tom Brady, Steph Curry), bought stadium naming rights, and pledged billions to charity through "Effective Altruism."

Behind the scenes, FTX was committing fraud. Customer deposits were secretly lent to Alameda Research (SBF's trading firm) for risky trades. When those trades went bad, FTX couldn't honor withdrawals.

November 2022: A leaked balance sheet revealed the fraud. Binance announced it would sell its FTX holdings. A bank run began. FTX halted withdrawals on November 8. On November 11, FTX filed for bankruptcy, revealing an $8 billion hole in customer funds.

SBF was arrested in the Bahamas and extradited to the US. In November 2023, he was convicted of fraud and conspiracy, facing decades in prison.

Lessons:

  • "Not your keys, not your coins"—self-custody matters
  • Celebrity endorsements and marketing don't equal legitimacy
  • Centralized exchanges pose custodial risk
  • Proof of reserves and audits are essential (FTX had neither)
  • Regulatory oversight exists for good reasons

FTX's collapse was crypto's Enron moment—a wake-up call about centralization risk and the importance of decentralization.

hacks_rugs.title: Hacks, Exploits, and Rug Pulls
hacks_rugs.content:
Crypto's history is littered with hacks and scams. Understanding these patterns helps you avoid becoming a victim.

Major DeFi Hacks:

  • Poly Network (August 2021): $611 million stolen across multiple chains. The hacker later returned the funds, calling it a white-hat exercise.
  • Ronin Bridge (March 2022): $624 million stolen through compromised validator keys. The attack targeted Axie Infinity's sidechain.
  • Wormhole Bridge (February 2022): $326 million stolen through a signature verification exploit.

Famous Rug Pulls:

  • Squid Game Token (November 2021): Creators prevented selling, pumped the price through FOMO, then drained liquidity. Price went from $0.01 to $2,856 to $0 in days.
  • OneCoin (2014-2019): Not technically crypto (no blockchain), but claimed to be. Scammed investors out of $4+ billion before collapsing.

Protection Strategies:

  • Verify contracts on block explorers
  • Check for audits (but don't trust them blindly)
  • Look for liquidity locks and team vesting
  • Be suspicious of anonymous teams and unrealistic promises
  • Start small—never invest more than you can afford to lose
  • Use hardware wallets for significant holdings

legendary_factors.title: What Makes a Token Legendary?
legendary_factors.content: Looking across successful projects, certain patterns emerge. Understanding what makes tokens legendary helps identify future winners and avoid failures.

innovation.title: Real Innovation vs Hype
innovation.content:
Legendary projects solve real problems with novel approaches:

Bitcoin: Solved digital scarcity without central authority
Ethereum: Enabled programmable money and unstoppable applications
Uniswap: Made decentralized trading actually work at scale
Aave: Pioneered flash loans and adaptive interest rates

Contrast this with projects that just copied existing ideas or relied purely on marketing. Innovation doesn't guarantee success, but lack of innovation almost guarantees eventual failure.

The Innovation Checklist:

  • Does this solve a real problem?
  • Is the solution technically novel or just marketing?
  • Can it work long-term without unsustainable incentives?
  • Does it create genuine value or just extract it from later users?

community.title: Community and Network Effects
community.content:
Technology alone isn't enough—legendary projects build passionate communities:

Bitcoin: Religious devotion to decentralization and fixed supply
Ethereum: Developers building unstoppable applications
BAYC: Celebrity endorsements and exclusive club culture
Solana: Community that rebuilt after FTX collapse

Strong communities provide resilience during bear markets, word-of-mouth marketing during growth, and collective problem-solving during crises.

Community Red Flags:

  • Cultish behavior suppressing legitimate criticism
  • Community driven by price discussion only ("wen moon")
  • Hostile to newcomers asking questions
  • Leaders promising guaranteed returns

Healthy communities debate, build, and support each other. Toxic communities pump, attack critics, and collapse when prices fall.

lessons.title: Timeless Lessons for Investors and Builders
lessons.content:
For Investors:

  • Timing matters, but not as much as fundamentals: Bitcoin bought at any point before 2021 was profitable by 2024
  • Diversify: Even legendary projects have 80%+ drawdowns
  • Self-custody for significant holdings: FTX proved that exchanges can fail
  • Understand what you own: If you can't explain why a token has value, you're gambling
  • Bear markets create opportunities: Legendary projects often launch in bear markets

For Builders:

  • Solve real problems: Hype fades, utility endures
  • Build in public: Open source and transparency create trust
  • Iterate based on usage: Aave and Uniswap constantly evolved based on user needs
  • Incentives matter: Make sure your tokenomics are sustainable beyond initial hype
  • Survive long enough to succeed: Ethereum took years to find product-market fit

Universal Truths:

  • Innovation compounds—today's projects build on yesterday's breakthroughs
  • Failures teach more than successes—learn from Luna, FTX, and The DAO
  • Decentralization is more than technology—it's philosophy and resilience
  • The most legendary projects often seem crazy at first
  • Respect the history—understanding the past helps navigate the future

genesis_block.definition: The first block in a blockchain. Bitcoin's genesis block was mined by Satoshi Nakamoto on January 3, 2009, containing a message about bank bailouts.

whitepaper.definition: A technical document describing a cryptocurrency's vision, technology, and implementation. Bitcoin's whitepaper by Satoshi Nakamoto is the foundational crypto document.

ico.definition: A fundraising method where projects sell tokens to early investors. Ethereum's 2014 ICO raised $18 million. The 2017 ICO boom also spawned countless scams.

hard_fork.definition: A backward-incompatible blockchain upgrade that splits the chain. Ethereum's hard fork after The DAO hack created Ethereum and Ethereum Classic.

defi_summer.definition: Summer 2020 when DeFi exploded in popularity. Compound's COMP token launch sparked yield farming mania, with billions flowing into DeFi protocols.

yield_farming.definition: Strategically moving crypto assets between protocols to maximize returns, often earning both interest and governance tokens as rewards.

nft.definition: A unique digital token representing ownership of a specific asset. Unlike cryptocurrencies, NFTs are not interchangeable—each one is unique.

blue_chip.definition: Established NFT collections with strong track records, like CryptoPunks and BAYC. Blue-chips hold value better during market downturns.

l1.definition: A base blockchain like Ethereum, Bitcoin, or Solana. L1s have their own consensus mechanism and don't depend on other chains.

l2.definition: A scaling solution built on top of an L1 blockchain. L2s process transactions off-chain but inherit the L1's security. Examples: Arbitrum, Optimism.

rollup.definition: A type of L2 that executes transactions off-chain but posts data to L1 for security. Optimistic rollups (Arbitrum) and ZK-rollups (zkSync) are the main types.

stablecoin.definition: A cryptocurrency designed to maintain a stable value, typically $1 USD. Types include fiat-backed (USDC), crypto-backed (DAI), and algorithmic (failed: UST).

depeg.definition: When a stablecoin loses its intended peg to $1. Small depegs are normal; large depegs (like UST's) can trigger death spirals.

rug_pull.definition: When developers drain liquidity or steal user funds and disappear. Named after "pulling the rug" out from under investors. Common in low-quality projects.
